name: let
description: Declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned but not redeclared in the same scope.
example: let count = 1; count = 2; // ok
notes: Unlike var, let is not hoisted to a usable state — accessing it before declaration throws a ReferenceError (the "temporal dead zone").

name: const
description: Declares a block-scoped variable whose binding cannot be reassigned after initialization.
example: const PI = 3.14; PI = 3; // TypeError
notes: const prevents reassignment, not mutation — const obj = {} still allows obj.key = 'x'.

name: Arrow Functions
description: A concise function syntax that does not bind its own `this`, `arguments`, or `super`, instead inheriting them from the enclosing scope.
example: const add = (a, b) => a + b; add(2, 3); // 5
notes: Not suitable as object methods that need their own `this`, or as constructors — they cannot be used with `new`.

name: Template Literals
description: String literals delimited by backticks that allow embedded expressions and multi-line strings.
example: const name = 'Sam'; `Hello, ${name}!`; // 'Hello, Sam!'
notes: Also support tagged templates: fn`text ${value}` passes the pieces to a custom function.

name: Array Destructuring
description: Unpacks values from an array into distinct variables based on position.
example: const [first, second] = [1, 2, 3]; // first = 1, second = 2
notes: Supports skipping elements ([, second]) and default values ([a = 10] = []).

name: Object Destructuring
description: Unpacks properties from an object into distinct variables based on property name, with optional renaming and defaults.
example: const { name, age = 30 } = { name: 'Sam' }; // name = 'Sam', age = 30
notes: Commonly used for destructuring function parameters, e.g. function greet({ name }) { ... }.

name: Spread Operator
description: Expands an iterable (array, string) or an object's own enumerable properties into individual elements or key-value pairs.
notes: Performs a shallow copy — commonly used for immutable updates like { ...state, key: value }.

name: Rest Parameters
description: Collects all remaining arguments passed to a function into a real array, instead of using the array-like `arguments` object.
example: function sum(...nums) { return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); } sum(1, 2, 3); // 6
notes: Must be the last parameter in the function signature; also works in destructuring, e.g. const [first, ...others] = arr.

name: Default Parameters
description: Allows named parameters to be initialized with default values if no value or undefined is passed.
example: function greet(name = 'Guest') { return `Hi, ${name}`; } greet(); // 'Hi, Guest'
notes: Default values are evaluated at call time and can reference earlier parameters.

name: Classes
description: Syntactic sugar over JavaScript's prototype-based inheritance, providing a cleaner syntax for creating objects and handling inheritance.
example: class Point { constructor(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } }
notes: Class declarations are not hoisted the way function declarations are — they exist in the temporal dead zone until evaluated.

name: Class Inheritance (extends/super)
syntax: class Child extends Parent { constructor() { super(); } }
description: Lets one class inherit properties and methods from another using extends, with super() used to call the parent constructor.
example: class Animal { speak() { return 'sound'; } } class Dog extends Animal { speak() { return 'bark'; } }
notes: super() must be called before `this` can be used in a subclass constructor.

name: ES Modules (import/export)
syntax: export const value = 1; / import { value } from './module.js';
description: The standard system for splitting JavaScript code into reusable, statically-analyzable files that explicitly declare their dependencies.
notes: Supports named exports and a single default export per module (export default ...).

name: Optional Chaining (?.)
description: Accesses a deeply nested property without throwing an error if an intermediate property is null or undefined.
example: const city = user?.address?.city; // undefined instead of throwing, if address is missing
notes: Short-circuits and returns undefined as soon as it hits a nullish value, without evaluating the rest of the chain.

name: Nullish Coalescing (??)
description: Returns the right-hand operand only when the left-hand operand is null or undefined, unlike || which also treats 0, '', and false as absent.
example: const count = 0 ?? 5; // 0 (|| would incorrectly give 5)
notes: Cannot be directly combined with && or || without parentheses due to operator precedence rules.

name: Map
description: A collection of key-value pairs where keys can be of any type (including objects), and insertion order is preserved.
example: const m = new Map(); m.set('a', 1); m.get('a'); // 1
notes: Unlike plain objects, Map keys aren't coerced to strings and Map has a built-in .size property.

name: Set
description: A collection of unique values of any type, with insertion order preserved and no duplicate entries allowed.
notes: A common idiom for deduplicating an array: [...new Set(array)].

name: Symbol
description: A primitive data type whose values are unique and immutable, often used as collision-free object property keys.
example: const id = Symbol('id'); const obj = { [id]: 123 };
notes: Symbol properties are excluded from Object.keys(), JSON.stringify(), and for...in loops.

name: Generator Functions
description: Functions that can be paused and resumed, producing a sequence of values over multiple calls via the yield keyword.
example: function* count() { yield 1; yield 2; } const it = count(); it.next(); // { value: 1, done: false }
notes: Generators return an iterator, making them useful for lazy sequences and custom iteration protocols.

name: Computed Property Names
description: Allows an object property's key to be computed dynamically from an expression at object-literal creation time.
example: const key = 'name'; const obj = { [key]: 'Sam' }; // { name: 'Sam' }

name: Shorthand Property Names
description: Lets you create an object property using a variable's name as the key and its value as the property value, without repeating the name.
example: const name = 'Sam'; const age = 30; const person = { name, age }; // { name: 'Sam', age: 30 }
notes: Also applies to method definitions: { greet() { ... } } instead of { greet: function() { ... } }.
